name: Write a tiny file
intro: A variable holds a value while a program runs. A file holds named content you can open again. Here you will practise real Python file operations in a temporary browser workspace. Files reset every Run; they are not saved to your phone.
prompt: Use with open("yourname.txt", "w") as a file variable. Write a nonempty string inside, then print a message outside the block.
hint:
with open("note.txt", "w") as note:
    note.write("Hi")
print("Written")
why: You used write a tiny file in working Python.

name: Read what you wrote
intro: Opening in "r" mode means read, not replace. read() returns the file content as a string. Write a practice file first, then reopen the SAME filename to read it, all in one Run.
prompt: Write a nonempty string to a file with "w". Reopen that same filename with "r", read its content, and print the content.
hint:
with open("note.txt", "w") as note:
    note.write("Hello")
with open("note.txt", "r") as note:
    message = note.read()
print(message)
why: You used read what you wrote in working Python.

name: Put text on new lines
intro: A newline moves the next character to a new line. Inside a Python string, backslash followed by n (\n) represents one newline character. Use it to store several lines in one file.
prompt: Write a string containing \n between two words to a file. Reopen it in "r" mode and print the read content.
hint:
with open("menu.txt", "w") as menu:
    menu.write("Tea\nCake")
with open("menu.txt", "r") as menu:
    text = menu.read()
print(text)
why: You used put text on new lines in working Python.

name: Keep the old text
intro: Append means add at the end without erasing what is already there. Mode "a" opens a file for appending. It also creates the file if it is missing.
prompt: Write starting text with "w", add different nonempty text to the same file with "a", then reopen with "r" and print the read content.
hint:
with open("note.txt", "w") as note:
    note.write("Tea")
with open("note.txt", "a") as note:
    note.write(" and cake")
with open("note.txt", "r") as note:
    text = note.read()
print(text)
why: You used keep the old text in working Python.

name: Read one line at a time
intro: A file can be looped over. Each turn gives the next line as text. This is useful for a list of notes without reading the whole file into one string first.
prompt: Create a file containing two lines using \n. Reopen in "r" mode, loop over the open file and print each loop variable with end="".
hint:
with open("list.txt", "w") as note:
    note.write("Tea\nCake\n")
with open("list.txt", "r") as note:
    for line in note:
        print(line, end="")
why: You used read one line at a time in working Python.

name: Count lines in a file
intro: Combine a file loop with a counter. Start a count at 0, add 1 for each line, then show the count after closing the file. This counts lines, not words or characters.
prompt: Write a file with two lines, reopen it in "r", loop through it and increase a counter from 0 by 1 each turn. Print the final counter after the loop.
hint:
with open("list.txt", "w") as note:
    note.write("Tea\nCake\n")
count = 0
with open("list.txt", "r") as note:
    for line in note:
        count = count + 1
print(count)
why: You used count lines in a file in working Python.

name: Build a tiny notebook
intro: Make a two-entry notebook using the file skills you now know: write, append, reopen, then loop through the lines. Each run builds a fresh practice notebook.
prompt: Write one line with "w" and append another with "a" to the same file. Include \n in each entry. Reopen with "r", loop over the file, and print each entry with end="".
hint:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as notes:
    notes.write("Learn Python\n")
with open("notes.txt", "a") as notes:
    notes.write("Practise daily\n")
with open("notes.txt", "r") as notes:
    for entry in notes:
        print(entry, end="")
why: You used build a tiny notebook in working Python.
